claims.text: Introducing TiC particles into a high-entropy-alloy coating will improve its wear resistance.
The proposed intervention is the introduction of TiC particles into an otherwise TiC-free high-entropy-alloy coating.
The wear-resistance improvement will hold from room temperature through 800 °C.
The wear-resistance improvement will hold under dry sliding.
Introducing TiC particles will cause formation of a strong and deformable oxide nanocomposite surface layer.
A strong and deformable oxide nanocomposite surface layer can provide reactive wear protection.
The oxide nanocomposite layer reduces wear by accommodating plastic strain without cracking or localized brittle fracture.
The TiC-modified coating will have a wear rate at least 77% lower than the unmodified coating.
The expected benefit is bounded or may not hold above 800 °C or under high-stress conditions.
The exact mechanism of reactive wear protection in the proposed TiC-modified coating is unknown.
The optimal amount of TiC for maximum wear resistance is unknown.
A comparative dry-sliding test at room temperature and 800 °C can test the modified coating against an otherwise unmodified coating.
Failure of the modified coating to show a significantly lower wear rate than the unmodified coating would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The mechanism is stated specifically as oxide-layer-mediated strain accommodation, while the uncertainty field says the exact reactive-wear-protection mechanism is unknown.

The prediction requires at least a 77% wear-rate reduction, but the falsification rule rejects the hypothesis only when there is no significant reduction. A significant reduction smaller than 77% would violate the quantitative prediction without triggering the stated rule.
